entries.topic: Stop distance vs. holding horizon: the √t noise band, and why entry location (not stop width) is the binding lever on multi-week swings
entries.summary: A stop has one job: fire on evidence the thesis broke, not on ordinary noise. Kaminski & Lo (SIFR RR 63, 2008; J. Financial Markets 18(C):234-254, 2014) prove that under a random walk, stop-loss rules ALWAYS decrease expected return; they only add value when returns exhibit momentum/positive serial correlation, generating what they call a 'stopping premium' proportional to return persistence (empirically 50-100bp/month during stop-out periods, US equities 1950-2004). So a stop placed inside the random-walk noise band is a pure expected-return tax. The quantitative half comes from volatility scaling: noise excursion grows with the SQUARE ROOT of time, so a stop sized off a one-day ATR is roughly √N too tight for an N-day hold (√45 ≈ 6.7). Danielsson & Zigrand (J. Banking & Finance 30(10):2701-2713, 2006) show the √t rule is only valid under iid normal returns and under jump diffusion 'leads to a systematic underestimation of risk, whereby the degree of underestimation worsens with the time horizon [and] the jump intensity' — so for equities with earnings inside the horizon, ATR×√N is a FLOOR on the noise band, not a ceiling. The decisive consequence: NO static entry stop inside a 15% cap can cover a 45-day noise band. This is not a reason to widen stops (the cap and the 2:1 RR floor forbid it) — it is the proof that stop width is not the free lever. Entry location is. The stop must only survive until the thesis STARTS working, which is why the Chandelier Exit (verified formula
key_points: Kaminski & Lo: under a random walk stops ALWAYS reduce expected return; they only pay when momentum/serial correlation is present. A stop inside the noise band is a pure tax.
Noise scales with √t: a 1-day ATR-based stop is ~√N too tight for an N-day hold (√45 ≈ 6.7). The min_stop_distance_pct floor is a ONE-DAY band, not a horizon band.
Danielsson & Zigrand: under jumps the √t rule UNDERSTATES risk, and worsens with horizon length — so ATR×√N is a floor on the true band, not a ceiling.
Therefore no static entry stop within the 15% cap can cover a 45-day noise band. Stop width is not the lever; ENTRY LOCATION is.
The stop must cover the noise band of the time until the thesis starts working (≈ATR×√days_to_catalyst), not the full horizon. Near catalyst + entry at support = a survivable stop.
Chandelier anchors to the 22-day HIGH, not entry (22d High − 3×ATR), precisely because a moving anchor re-measures the band as the trade works. Verified formula.
Gap risk means 1R is not a guaranteed loss: SEC says a stop is a trigger, not a fill price. DELL realized -1.43R through a 408 stop. Budget realized risk at ~1.3-1.5R on jump-prone names.
MAE (tighten stops to where winners live) contradicts the above but needs ~100 trades; at 2 closed trades it is unusable — sample-size rules outrank it.
entries.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, run the horizon-vs-noise test: compare my stop distance (%) against the name's daily ATR% × √(days until the nearest real catalyst) — NOT the full holding_horizon_days. If the stop is inside that band, the setup is asking a coin-flip to pay me: either move the entry down near the structural swing low so the same stop sits beyond the band, shorten the stated horizon to match what the stop can actually survive, or pass. Never widen the stop to fix this — the 15% cap and the 2:1 RR floor make wide stops fail geometry anyway, and stop_engineering's min_stop_distance_pct is a ONE-DAY floor that I must stop treating as horizon-adequate. Prefer setups where the catalyst is near and the entry is at support, since both shrink the noise the stop must clear; a 40-day thesis with no catalyst for three weeks needs ~4×ATR of room just to survive to its own event, which usually breaches the cap and is a pass. Because the chandelier trail re-anchors to the high, my job at entry is only to buy the trade time to get moving — so on names with earnings inside the horizon or a history of gaps, size on ~1.3-1.5R of realized risk rather than the nominal 1% (DELL filled 4.5% through its st

Daníelsson, J. & Zigrand, J-P., 'On Time-Scaling of Risk and the Square-Root-Of-Time Rule', Journal of Banking & Finance 30(10):2701-2713 (2006) — https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=567123

entries.topic: Correlation-adjusted position sizing: co-moving names are one bet (the effective-number-of-bets collapse), not many, and why that governs portfolio heat and the theme-risk cap
entries.summary: Diversification by COUNT is an illusion; only diversification by uncorrelated risk FACTORS reduces risk. For N equally-sized positions each with volatility sigma and pairwise correlation rho, portfolio volatility is sigma*sqrt([1+(N-1)*rho]/N): at rho=0 that is sigma/sqrt(N) (full benefit), but at rho->1 it goes to sigma, i.e. the N positions behave as ONE. The clean summary statistic is the effective number of independent bets, N_eff ~= N/[1+(N-1)*rho]; two names at rho~0.85 give N_eff~1.08 -- essentially a single bet. That is exactly my realized loss history: DELL and HPE were two tickers on ONE hyperscaler_server_capex driver, so a Meta-overbuild headline took both out at once, and my '2 positions' were 1 correlated bet the whole time. Attilio Meucci's Effective Number of Bets (exponential Shannon entropy of the diversification distribution) makes the same point formally: hidden correlation makes a book that LOOKS like N holdings act like ~1 exposure to one factor, and PCA can even hide this (minimum-torsion/factor framing is needed to see it). The Turtle system encoded the practitioner version as hard unit caps -- 4 units single market, 6 closely-correlated, 10 loosely, 12 in one direction -- precisely so a cluster of correlated trades could not become one oversized bet. Two cautions from the sources: (1) correlations RISE toward 1 in exactly the tail shock you are stopping for, so a benign-looking rho understates joint downside; (2) correlated stops fire and GAP together
key_points: Portfolio vol for N equal positions = sigma*sqrt([1+(N-1)*rho]/N); as rho->1 the whole book collapses to one position's risk. Two 20%-vol names equal-weight: 14.1% vol at rho=0 vs 20% at rho=1 -- the entire benefit is gone.
Effective number of independent bets N_eff ~= N/[1+(N-1)*rho]; two names at rho~0.85 = ~1.08 bets. DELL+HPE was arithmetically one bet, and it is my only realized-loss cluster.

The diagnostic question (per practitioners): 'what single event would make most of my open positions lose at once?' If positions co-move >~0.7 or share a demand_driver, they are ONE bet regardless of ticker count or GICS label.

Meucci's ENB / diversification ratio: count-based diversification is meaningless; only exposure to uncorrelated factors counts, and hidden correlation can make an apparently-diversified book a concentrated one-factor bet.
Turtle caps (4 single / 6 closely-correlated / 10 loosely / 12 one direction units) are the practitioner encoding of 'do not let correlated trades stack into one oversized bet.'

Tail behavior is worse than the average rho suggests: correlations spike toward 1 in a shock, and correlated stops fire and gap together -- so sizing, not the stop, is the defense against a correlated gap-through (DELL filled ~4.5% past its stop).

Honesty check: a common 'effective risk = risk*sqrt(N*rho)' blog example (6x1% at 0.85 -> 13.6%) is inconsistent -- combined risk cannot exceed the sum of parts; use the portfolio-variance identity instead.
entries.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, run the one-bet test using portfolio_risk and the demand_driver_map: if the candidate shares a holding's demand_driver OR shows corr_to_book > ~0.7, treat it as ADDING to an existing bet, not opening a new one -- size the pair against the THEME RISK <= 2% cap as a single position, never as two independent 1% risks (this is the DELL+HPE lesson made quantitative). When shared_left_tail is true, actively prefer a low/negative corr_to_book diversifier (diversifier=true) over a higher-conviction clone of what I already own, because at book level the clone adds almost no independent bet. Cite the actual number ('~0.85 correlated to DELL, N_eff ~1.1, so this is one hyperscaler_server_capex bet in two tickers'), not a vibe, and let the factor-stack cap / factor_response gate do its job rather than relabeling a name into a cheaper theme bucket. Because correlations rise and stops gap together in the exact shock I am stopped for, on a correlated add I size on realized (gap-adjusted) risk -- lean to ~1.3-1.5R of modelled slippage and toward the lower end of size -- rather than assuming the stop caps the loss. Net rule: diversify by demand_driver, not by ticker count; if I cann

Attilio Meucci, 'Managing Diversification' (Effective Number of Bets): https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1358533 ; Portfolio Optimizer explainer: https://portfoliooptimizer.io/blog/the-effective-number-of-bets-measuring-portfolio-diversification/

entries.topic: The pullback-continuation entry in a leading uptrend: buying the low-volume ('no-supply') dip to structural support instead of chasing the fresh high
entries.summary: The pullback-continuation setup buys a temporary dip inside an established uptrend rather than chasing a new high. It works because two well-documented return patterns run on different clocks: medium-term momentum persists over roughly 3-12 months while short-term returns (days to a few weeks) mean-revert (the short-term reversal effect, Blitz/Huij, Alpha Architect summaries). Buying the short-term dip in a medium-term leader therefore rides the durable trend while getting a better price and a tighter stop. The whole craft is separating a HEALTHY pullback -- shallow, orderly, on DRYING volume, the Wyckoff/VSA 'no supply' bar where professionals simply stop selling -- from a REVERSAL, which is sharp, wide-range, and comes on HIGH volume that breaks structure ('supply'). Volume is the tell, not price alone. Minervini's version: after a valid advance a healthy pullback retraces modestly (~8-10% max, or back to a rising 50-DMA), volume contracts into the dip and re-expands on the resumption; common support zones are the 20-EMA, 50-DMA, and the 38-62% Fibonacci band. Critically, the entry is the RESUMPTION, not the dip itself -- you wait for volume to dry up and then a confirming up-move, you do not catch the falling knife. This is the one thing my own 12-year ablation confirmed: no_supply_pullback scored +0.22pp (21d) / +0.25pp (63d), the only positive read among ~25 indicators tested, measured on names already above their 200-DMA. Reported win rates vary wildly and the high ones
key_points: Two clocks: 3-12mo momentum persists while days-to-weeks returns revert (short-term reversal) -- a pullback in a leader rides the trend at a better price and a tighter stop.

Volume is the discriminator: healthy pullback = shallow, orderly, volume DRYING UP (Wyckoff 'no supply'); reversal = sharp, wide-range, HIGH volume breaking support. A high-volume dip is supply -- pass.
Depth/zone guides: after a valid advance ~8-10% max or back to a rising 50-DMA; support at the 20-EMA, 50-DMA, or 38-62% Fibonacci retracement.
Enter the RESUMPTION, not the dip: wait for volume to dry up, then a confirming up-bar / short-term-level reclaim -- never buy the falling knife.
My only ablation-confirmed edge: no_supply_pullback +0.22pp (21d)/+0.25pp (63d) on names above the 200-DMA -- this playbook is the one I have first-party evidence for.
Reconciles my own bundle: high-ADX breakouts measured -0.35pp (fail) but the low-volume pullback measured positive -- in an extended trend, buy the orderly dip, don't chase the breakout.
Win rates: distrust the '82%' SEO claim; credible ~55-65% for MA-reversion pullbacks, weaker in low-turnover names and stretched momentum-gap conditions -- real edge, not universal.
Buying at support satisfies KB-2388376284: the same stop then sits beyond the sqrt-t noise band, so entry location -- not stop width -- carries the risk.
entries.how_to_apply: When a universe leader (above a rising 50/200-DMA, positive rel_strength_1m and 3m vs SPY) pulls back, treat it as a BUY candidate only when the dip is orderly AND volume_signal reads no_supply_pullback -- my one ablation-confirmed tell; a high-volume, wide-range dip is supply, so pass. Do not buy the dip itself: wait for volume to dry up and a resumption bar (reclaim of a short-term level or a pocket-pivot-style up day), which is the concrete fix for my ANET regret_miss where I watched the pullback and never entered. Anchor the stop just below the pullback's swing low or the named anchored_vwap level so the same stop sits beyond the noise band per KB-2388376284, hold the 2:1 RR floor honestly, and let the chandelier trail run the winner rather than tightening early. Prefer pullbacks with a catalyst inside a short window so entry-to-event noise is small, and size the initial entry at 50-70% then scale in only on confirmed strength. In an already-extended, high-ADX leader this low-volume pullback -- not the fresh breakout my own data shows fails at ADX>25 -- is where the fat pitch lives.

entries.topic: Exit on pre-committed invalidators, not real-time conviction: the disposition effect, 'resulting', and why the written plan (not the mood) must license every early exit
entries.summary: My single binding process_fail is HPE: I closed a LOSING position ahead of its stop on a 'conviction crack,' graded process_fail with tag missing_invalidators_on_plan. The behavioral literature explains why that class of decision loses systematically. Odean's canonical study of 10,000 brokerage accounts (Journal of Finance 53:1775-1798, 1998) documents the disposition effect: investors are 1.5-2x more likely to sell a winner than a loser, and crucially this is NOT justified by subsequent returns - the losers they clung to did not go on to outperform, so the discretionary exit judgment was simply wrong on average. The practitioner consensus fix is pre-commitment: a 1991 study found the disposition effect weakens sharply when people sell at predetermined rules/intervals instead of discretionarily, and the reliable antidotes are predefined exit rules set BEFORE entry, mechanical stop/target execution, and documenting the rationale so the exit is a rule-check rather than a fresh emotional decision. Annie Duke's 'resulting' sharpens this: judging a decision by its outcome corrupts learning, so you must write the reasoning and the expected outcome distribution up front and grade the exit against THAT, not against the P&L - which is exactly why DELL (stop fired as planned, still a loss) is a process_win while HPE (discretionary, happened to save a few dollars) is a process_fail. The honest nuance: my HPE error was not the classic disposition effect (I cut a loser early, I didn't hol
key_points: Odean 1998 (JoF 53:1775-1798): the disposition effect is real and NOT vindicated by later returns - discretionary 'when to exit' judgment loses on average, so it must be replaced by rules.
Pre-commitment is the measured fix: the disposition effect weakens when exits fire on predetermined rules; predefined criteria + mechanical execution + written rationale beat real-time discretion.

Duke's 'resulting': grade the exit against the plan you wrote at entry, never against the P&L - a planned stop-loss is a process_win (DELL), a discretionary exit is a process_fail even if it saved money (HPE).
My HPE loss wasn't classic disposition effect (I cut a loser early) but the same root: emotion overrode a plan that had no written invalidators to test the exit against.
Action bias and omission bias are the same disease, sign-flipped: over-trading AND the 6-day unwind paralysis both come from letting an emotional state, not the written bar, decide.
The antidote to cutting winners early is mechanical: sell_fraction partials at >=2R plus the chandelier trail, so the rule (not the itch to lock in) manages the runner.
Silence-of-invalidators is a HOLD signal: if no written invalidator fired, 'conviction cracked' or 'the tape feels bad' is not a licensed reason to exit before stop/target/horizon.
entries.how_to_apply: Treat the validator-enforced thesis_invalidators (invalidating_print, invalidating_structure, time_box) as the ONLY licensed early-exit reasons: before closing any holding ahead of its stop, name which specific invalidator fired and cite the observable print or structure - if none did and it is only conviction wobble, HOLD and let the stop/chandelier trail do its job, because that is the exact HPE process_fail I must not repeat. Grade every exit against the entry plan, not the P&L (Duke's resulting): a stop firing as written is a process_win even at a loss, a discretionary save is a process_fail. For winners, beat the cut-them-early disposition reflex mechanically - bank with sell_fraction (~0.4-0.6) at >=2R and trail the rest under structure while invalidators stay clear, per KB-2388376284's chandelier point and the runner playbook. Apply the same rule to the paralysis mirror-error: an unwind is a code-applied half-size haircut, not a trading halt, so if a setup clears the fat-pitch bar and validator floors honestly I take it, and if it does not I pass on its own merits - I never let a standing condition (unwind, thin tape, last week's loss) become an unwritten veto, and I never f
sources: Odean, T. (1998), 'Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?', Journal of Finance 53:1775-1798 (faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/odean/papers current versions/areinvestorsreluctant.pdf; SSRN abstract_id=94142)

Enlightened Stock Trading, 'The Disposition Effect in Trading: How to Fix This Costly Bias' (enlightenedstocktrading.com/disposition-effect-in-trading/) - predefined exit rules, automation, documented rationale; ~3-5%/yr return cost cited in practitioner literature

Annie Duke, 'Thinking in Bets' / 'resulting' - separating decision quality from outcome quality (investinglive.com/Education/annie-duke-on-the-investing-mistakes...; tomtunguz.com/outcome-quality-decision-quality/)
Action bias and omission bias in trading (effectiviology.com/action-bias/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omission_bias) - real-money accounts trade more and underperform; inaction is the mirror error

entries.topic: Estimate-revision momentum: how upward EPS/revenue revision breadth leads price via the post-forecast-revision drift, and why breadth + price-confirmation beats a lone divergence
entries.summary: Analyst estimate revisions are a genuine, well-documented fundamental predictor: prices underreact to revisions and DRIFT in their direction for roughly six months (the post-forecast-revision drift, PFRD). Old evidence (Givoly/Lakonishok-era) put the up-minus-down revision portfolio spread near ~3% annually, and later work finds aggregated revisions can predict post-earnings-announcement returns as well as or better than the earnings surprise itself. The mechanism is the reason it persists and is the key to trading it: the DIRECTION of revisions is far more persistent than the direction of returns because analysts themselves underreact — anchoring-and-adjustment and herding make them revise incrementally and insufficiently, so a first up-revision statistically predicts more up-revisions (Chen et al. 2020, JBFA). Signal quality is not uniform. A single revision is mostly noise, and noise/bias in analyst forecasts rises with the forecast horizon (Noise in Expectations, RFS 2024), so BREADTH — how many analysts are raising vs cutting over ~100 days — and NEAR-TERM (next-quarter/next-FY) revisions carry the real signal, not one far-out number. Consistency matters more than magnitude: high-innovation revisions that are CONSISTENT with the prior trend and with price action drive more drift than larger 'reversal' revisions that fight the tape (Chen 2025), and revisions that merely drift toward existing consensus ('low-innovation') carry little information. Practitioners (Mill Street
key_points: PFRD is real and persistent: prices drift in the revision's direction for ~6 months; my 3-90d swing only needs to capture the front of a durable trend, which is favorable.
The tradeable core: revision DIRECTION is more persistent than return direction because analysts underreact/anchor/herd — a first up-revision predicts more up-revisions.
Use BREADTH (raisers minus cutters over ~100d), not a single estimate change; a lone revision is noise.
Prefer NEAR-TERM revisions (next-Q/next-FY); noise and bias grow with forecast horizon.
Consistency > magnitude: revisions that agree with the prior trend and price drive more drift than larger reversal revisions; revisions merely converging to consensus carry little info.
Highest-conviction setup = up-revision breadth CONFIRMED by constructive price (this is exactly my post_earnings_drift_candidate gap_held_revisions_up flag).

The revisions-up / price-weak divergence (MU) is the seductive trap: sometimes underreaction opportunity, sometimes price-knows-first; resolve by diagnosing why price is weak and waiting for price confirmation, not by buying estimates alone.
But do not reflexively SKIP the divergence either — that is my documented over-skip; watchlist it with a price-reclaim trigger and act when price confirms.
entries.how_to_apply: Treat fundamental_screen.top_upward_revisions and revision_direction=up / positive eps_growth_next_yr_pct as a real candidate lane, not background noise — this is the direct fix for repeatedly defaulting MU-type names to the watchlist and eating +15% regret_misses. When underwriting one, weight BREADTH of near-term (30-day EPS / next-Q) revisions over any single number, and require the revision trend to be consistent (up-revisions following up-revisions), because that persistence is where the edge lives. For the fat pitch, demand price CONFIRMATION of the fundamentals — positive rel_strength_1m/3m, no_supply_pullback or a reclaim — which is precisely the post_earnings_drift_candidate gap_held_revisions_up read; that revisions-and-price-AGREE case gets full weight and can clear the bar now. For the pure divergence (revisions up, price down, MU-style), do NOT buy estimates into a falling knife and do NOT reflexively skip: name in the thesis whether price weakness is temporary (cyclical/sector/tax/macro) or structural (ai_at_risk, cycle-peak earnings embedding the cycle continuing), put it on the watchlist with a specific price-reclaim trigger, and promote to BUY when price confirms —
sources: Chen, Narayanamoorthy, Sougiannis & Zhou (2020), 'Analyst Underreaction and the Post-Forecast Revision Drift', Journal of Business Finance & Accounting — https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2578757

Chen (2025), 'Analyst forecast revision consistency and reversal: Evidence of stock market efficiency', Journal of Corporate Accounting & Finance — https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcaf.22744
'The Value of Analyst Forecast Revisions' — https://escholarship.org/content/qt2r7980f3/qt2r7980f3_noSplash_c002fc5c3b5de2401d705fadd922a1f3.pdf
'Noise in Expectations: Evidence from Analyst Forecasts', Review of Financial Studies 37(5), 2024 — https://academic.oup.com/rfs/article/37/5/1494/7461199

entries.topic: The options-implied expected move and earnings IV crush: reading options_signals to time swing entries around binary prints, and why the implied move is a market-priced noise band
entries.summary: Options price a stock's expected move as Price × IV × √(DTE/365) ≈ one standard deviation; a fast earnings shortcut is ~0.85 × the ATM front-month straddle (tastytrade uses a weighted straddle+strangle version). Empirically the stock stays inside that ±1σ band ~68-70% of the time, so the implied move is a genuine, horizon-scaled noise band — not a forecast of direction. Crucially it is priced too WIDE on average: implied vol exceeds realized vol by roughly 3-5 percentage points annualized (the volatility risk premium), and a CBOE study of ~10 years of S&P 500 earnings found the actual post-print move was SMALLER than the straddle-implied move in ~72% of cases. But the distribution has fat tails — the ~30% of moves that break the band include the outliers that gap through any stop (the SMCI ~20% preliminary-print pop is exactly this tail). Before a known binary event, front-month IV inflates and the term structure goes into BACKWARDATION (near-term IV > far-term); the moment the event resolves, IV crushes 30-50% (40-55% on high-IV names like NVDA/TSLA) within hours and the term structure normalizes. For a directional trader, holding a swing stop THROUGH a print means betting on a coin-flip gap you are not paid to take: the pre-print premium is a cost to option holders, but to an equity holder the print is just an un-stoppable jump on top of the normal diffusion. The cleaner trade is around it — enter 1-2 days after the print once the gap settles, IV has crushed, and the direct
key_points: Expected move = Price × IV × √(DTE/365) ≈ 1σ ≈ 0.85 × ATM straddle; stock stays inside it ~68-70% of the time — it's a horizon-scaled NOISE band, never a direction call.

The band is priced wide: IV > RV by ~3-5pp/yr (volatility risk premium); a CBOE 10-yr study found the real earnings move was smaller than implied ~72% of the time. But fat tails mean the ~30% of breaks contain the account-denting gaps.

Term-structure backwardation (front IV > back IV) + elevated iv_rank = an event premium is priced into the front month; this is the detector that a binary is coming even without a clean calendar date.
IV crush: front-month IV peaks the session before the print and drops 30-50% (40-55% on high-IV names) within hours; the term structure then normalizes.

A single-day earnings expected move is a DISCRETE jump layered on top of the diffusion noise band — no valid swing stop inside the 15% cap survives it, so the honest move is to trade AROUND the print, not through it.
Post-print entry (1-2 days later) lets the gap settle and IV crush, giving a fairer price with the binary removed — the same window where post_earnings_drift / gap_held_revisions_up pays.
Chasing the gap on the print bar is buying the fat-tail move with no clean stop; the disciplined re-entry is the light-volume retest (per KB-6241168493), not the climax bar.
entries.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, read options_signals.expected_move_pct and term_structure together with days_to_earnings: if a print (or a backwardation + high-iv_rank event premium) falls inside holding_horizon_days, default to trading AROUND it — either enter after the print once IV crushes and the gap settles, or shorten the horizon so the stop never has to survive the binary, because the earnings expected move is a discrete jump no ATR-floored stop inside the 15% cap can cover (this refines KB-2388376284: the implied move is a market-priced noise band, superior to ATR×√N, and stop_engineering already floors the stop at ½ the expected move — treat that as a one-day floor, not horizon-adequate through an event). Only hold through a print when the binary itself is the thesis (a stated drift/gap_held_revisions_up setup per KB-2596574918), and then size on gap-adjusted risk. Use term-structure backwardation and iv_rank as the detector that fired wrong on AMD — an elevated front-month event premium 5 days out means the setup is NOT live yet, so suppress the trigger until the event passes. entries.topic: Kelly-fraction intuition for the 1% risk budget: why deep-fractional Kelly is correct under parameter uncertainty, and how it explains the 2:1 RR floor and the conviction tier
entries.summary: The Kelly criterion f* = W - (1-W)/R maximizes long-run geometric growth (E[log wealth]) and outputs the fraction of capital to RISK - which maps exactly onto this system's 1%-of-equity, entry-to-stop budget. Running it on my own realistic parameters (2:1 RR floor so R is about 2, swing win rates 40-55% per CLAUDE.md) gives full-Kelly risk fractions of 10% (at 40% wins), 17.5% (45%), 25% (50%), and 32.5% (55%). So the 1% budget is roughly 1/10 to 1/30 of full Kelly - deeper than even quarter-Kelly - and that is correct, not timid, for three compounding reasons the literature is unanimous on. First, parameter uncertainty: MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba showed a 10% overestimate of edge causes about 50% overbetting at full Kelly, the penalty for overbetting FAR exceeds the cost of underbetting, and Thorp always ran fractional Kelly in practice; with only 2 closed trades my true edge is essentially unknown, and Kelly with unknown edge says bet near zero. Second, the growth-rate curve is a downward parabola g(c*f*) approximately (2c - c^2)*g_max: half-Kelly captures about 75% of maximum growth at half the position size, quarter-Kelly about 44%, growth hits ZERO at 2x Kelly, and beyond 2x it goes negative into near-certain ruin - so the over side has a cliff the under side does not, making underbetting strictly the safer error. Third, Kelly assumes independent bets; correlated simultaneous positions share ONE Kelly budget (the multivariate form is f* = inverse-covariance times excess return
key_points: Kelly f* = W - (1-W)/R outputs the fraction of capital to RISK, directly comparable to the 1% entry-to-stop budget; at R=2 and 40-55% win rates full Kelly is 10-32%, so 1% is ~1/10 to 1/30 of full Kelly - deep-fractional by design, not timidity.

Growth curve is a parabola: g(c*f*) approx (2c-c^2)*g_max. Half-Kelly = ~75% of max growth at half size; ZERO growth at 2x Kelly; negative beyond. Overbetting is strictly dominated - 1.5x Kelly gives the same growth as 0.5x with far more drawdown.

The overbetting penalty dwarfs the underbetting cost (MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba: a 10% edge overestimate -> ~50% overbet at full Kelly). Under uncertainty, fractional Kelly is roughly optimal and Thorp always used it - err LOW.

With only 2 closed trades my edge is unmeasured; Kelly with unknown edge says bet minimally. The 5/15-trade calibration thresholds are how the edge estimate sharpens enough to justify moving UP the fraction.
The 2:1 RR floor is Kelly-consistent: at R=1, f*=2W-1<=0 for W<=50%, so a 1:1 book has no Kelly edge - the floor exists so that even 40-45% win rates keep f* positive.

The conviction tier (1%->1.5%, gated on 15 trades AND a proven 55%+ win rate in the 0.70+ bucket) is a small, evidence-gated step up the Kelly fraction - Bayesian shrinkage that raises size on DATA, never on narrative.

Kelly assumes independent bets; correlated simultaneous positions share one budget (multivariate f* = Sigma^-1 (mu-r)). The 8% heat cap and 2% theme-risk cap ARE the portfolio-Kelly constraint - the quantitative reason co-moving names scale down (ties KB-1223831607).

Position size is fully determined by two levers: size = risk_budget / stop_distance. Kelly sets the numerator (how much edge justifies risking); the sqrt-t noise band (KB-2388376284) sets the denominator (where the stop sits). Neither alone sizes a trade.
entries.how_to_apply: Keep sizing every BUY at the 1% risk budget and read it as intentional deep-fractional Kelly, not caution to apologize for: with 2 closed trades my edge is unmeasured, so betting small IS the mathematically correct response to unknown edge, and I should stop treating the 1% floor as a bar that makes setups feel too small to bother taking. When tempted to argue for the conviction tier (1.5%), require what Kelly requires: a genuinely higher, PROVEN edge (the validator's 15 trades + 55% win rate in the 0.70+ bucket, confidence >=0.75, zero risk-desk haircut, corroborating evidence) - never step up the fraction on a narrative, because the overbetting penalty is asymmetric and a wrong edge estimate over-allocates hard. Treat the 2:1 RR floor as non-negotiable expectancy geometry, not paperwork: below it there is no positive Kelly fraction to size, so never widen a stop or inflate a target to scrape past it. On correlated adds, remember co-moving names share one Kelly budget - the 8% heat and 2% theme-risk caps are that constraint, so size the pair as one bet (KB-1223831607) rather than two independent 1% risks. entries.topic: Reading the consolidation base to define a precise, auditable pivot trigger — and why the throwback to the level, not the breakout through it, is the higher-expectancy swing entry
entries.summary: The base-and-pivot framework (O'Neil's cup-with-handle, Minervini's VCP) exists to convert a fuzzy 'wait for confirmation' into ONE auditable price level: the pivot — the base's prior peak / handle high, the last ceiling of overhead supply. A valid VCP base shows 2-3 successive contractions where BOTH price range AND volume tighten, each smaller than the last, signaling sellers drying up; the classic entry then buys as price clears the pivot on volume ~40-50% above average. But the empirical record undercuts the 'chase the volume breakout' half. Bulkowski's pattern database (reported ~40,000+ trades on thepatternsite.com; I could not fetch the primary page directly and cite these figures as reported by secondary summaries) finds throwbacks occur ~50-60% of the time overall and ~74% when the breakout comes on ABOVE-average volume, and that ~97% of upward-breakout pattern TYPES perform BETTER when no throwback occurs — the strongest breakouts run away and never offer a second chance, while high-volume 'confirmed' breakouts are precisely the ones that throw back most. My own 12-year ablation says the same from the entry side: confirmed_breakout (new 20d high on >=1.5x volume) scored -0.32pp ATR-matched at 21d and ADX>25 breakouts were negative in 10 of 12 years, while the low-volume no_supply_pullback was the ONE positive read (+0.22/+0.25pp). Practitioner consensus reconciles this: buying the throwback/retest to the pivot (now acting as support) on drying volume gives a better
key_points: The pivot is a precise, auditable level (base's prior peak / handle high, cross-checked vs anchored_vwap) — write THAT into would_buy_at, never a vague 'after confirmation'.
A valid VCP base = 2-3 successive contractions each tighter in range AND volume; the volume dry-up is the setup, clearing the pivot is only the trigger.

Bulkowski (reported): throwbacks ~50-60% overall, ~74% on above-average-volume breakouts; ~97% of upward pattern types perform better WITHOUT a throwback — high-volume 'confirmed' breakouts throw back most.
My own ablation agrees from the entry side: confirmed_breakout -0.32pp, ADX>25 breakouts negative 10/12 yrs; no_supply_pullback +0.22/+0.25pp is the only positive read among ~25 indicators.
Highest-expectancy entry here is the throwback/retest to the pivot on drying volume (better fill, tighter stop under the base, higher RR) — i.e. KB-6241168493, not the breakout chase.

The cost is real and must be sized around: the strongest ~26-40% of breakouts never retest, so waiting means missing some big winners; a 50-70% starter on the breakout + add on the retest is the compromise when a catalyst forces urgency.

Do NOT treat a light-volume ('unconfirmed') breakout as a veto — breakout volume carries no positive information either way in my data, and CLAUDE.md forbids using it to reject a thesis that stands on its own.
entries.how_to_apply: For every watchlist name, read its base and write the PIVOT — the prior peak / handle high, cross-checked against anchored_vwap — as the would_buy_at level, plus an explicit event-date gate when a catalyst window applies, which fixes the AMD compound-trigger-fired-5-days-early defect (LP-0693555695). Prefer the entry my own data rewards: the throwback to that pivot on drying, no_supply_pullback volume (KB-6241168493), with the stop just below the base low so it sits beyond the sqrt(t) noise band (KB-2388376284) and the 2:1 RR floor clears honestly because I am buying AT the level, not extended above it. Do not make the volume breakout my primary entry and do not reject a setup because its breakout was unconfirmed — confirmed_breakout scored -0.32pp and breakout volume is descriptive-only. When a genuine fat pitch is running away in a supportive tape with a catalyst forcing urgency, take a 50-70% starter on the breakout and add on the retest rather than chasing full size or missing it. Accept that some of the strongest breakouts never come back: that is the priced cost of the higher-RR retest entry, not a process failure — consistent with ~30% of my regret_misses being market-wide m

entries.topic: The catalyst-in-a-downtrend setup: why good news on a below-MA / near-52-week-low name has the WEAKEST expected drift, and the confirmation-gated re-entry that separates a real turn from a dead-cat bo
entries.summary: My biggest single cluster of shadow-book regret_misses is the same setup every time — a positive catalyst (beat-and-raise, raised guidance, insider cluster) on a name trading BELOW its 50/200-DMA, which I reject for 'lack of confirmation' and then never re-enter when confirmation arrives (CLS +10.5%, NOW +12%, IBM +11%, NOC, HCA, SMCI). The naive read is 'I was too cautious.' The evidence says the opposite about the SKIP and pinpoints my real error elsewhere. George, Hwang & Li (Anchoring, the 52-Week High and PEAD) find post-earnings drift is concentrated by nearness to the 52-week high: investors anchor on the high and underreact to GOOD news when a stock is NEAR its high (strong upward drift, the tradeable long), but that underreaction — and therefore the drift edge — is WEAKEST when the same good news lands on a name far from its high / near its low; the drift only re-ignites once the 52-week high (or the relevant overhead level) is reclaimed and 'the market wakes up.' So the best PEAD longs are good-news LEADERS, not good-news names in a downtrend. Bulkowski's dead-cat-bounce database says the same from the price side: large event declines (almost all company-specific bad-or-good-then-faded news) typically bounce ~50% of the drop on FADING volume, make a lower high, then resume the decline 'at a more leisurely rate.' Practitioner consensus (bear-market-rally and reversal writing, O'Neil's follow-through logic) converges on the tell: a dead-cat bounce fails at resistance
key_points: Academic core (George/Hwang/Li): good-news drift is STRONGEST near the 52-week high and WEAKEST near the low — so a catalyst on a below-MA/near-52w-low name is the low-edge PEAD cell, not a hidden gift; the edge re-ignites only when overhead resistance is reclaimed.

Bulkowski dead-cat-bounce data: big event declines usually bounce ~half on fading volume, form a lower high, then keep declining — chasing the first pop in a downtrend is statistically the wrong side.

Dead-cat-bounce vs real reversal, the checklist: FADE = lower high + shrinking volume + breaks prior low; TURN = higher-high-and-higher-low, successful retest of the low on LOWER volume, rising volume on advances, reclaim/hold above the declining 50-DMA.

O'Neil follow-through logic applied to a single name: don't try to catch the bottom; require a confirmation up-day that shows institutional accumulation (a reclaim held for 2-3 sessions on volume) before committing.

My real error was NOT the skip — it was rejecting-and-forgetting: no armed re-entry trigger, so when the turn confirmed I wasn't watching. The fix is a specific structural trigger on the watchlist, not a same-day chase.
This fills a genuine gap: KB-6241168493 (pullback-continuation) only covers names already ABOVE the 200-DMA; it says nothing about a name coming off a bottom, which is where these regrets live.
entries.how_to_apply: When a positive catalyst lands on a name trading below its 50/200-DMA (CLS/NOW/IBM/NOC pattern), do NOT chase the gap and do NOT reject-and-forget: put it on the watchlist with a would_buy_at written as an explicit change-of-character structure — a reclaim of the declining 50-DMA held 2-3 sessions on above-average volume, PLUS a higher-low that survives a retest of the bounce low on lighter volume — and only promote to BUY when that prints (refining KB-2596574918's 'buy on price confirmation' with the concrete structure, and extending KB-6241168493 to below-MA names). Weight the George/Hwang anchoring prior: rank good-news LEADERS near their highs above good-news names near their lows, because the drift edge is where the anchor is being broken, not where the stock is still deep in supply. Use volume as the arbiter per KB-6241168493 — fading volume into the bounce and a lower high is a dead-cat, so pass; rising volume on the reclaim plus a no_supply_pullback retest is the tradeable turn. Anchor the stop just below the retest's higher low (which by construction sits beyond the √t noise band, KB-2388376284) so the 2:1 RR clears honestly from a level, not from an extended chase; if a p

entries.topic: Market breadth as the regime aggression dial: participation, the divergence/thrust asymmetry, and why breadth is a CONDITION not a timing signal
entries.summary: Breadth measures how many stocks are PARTICIPATING, which no index level can reveal - an index at new highs on narrowing participation and one on broadening participation look identical in SPY but are different regimes. The classic bearish read is a breadth DIVERGENCE: the index prints a new high while the advance-decline line makes a lower high and the share of stocks above their 200-DMA falls, meaning the advance is being carried by fewer, larger names. Documented cases precede 1987, 2000, 2007 and 2021 tops (the NYSE A-D line peaked nearly two years before the 2000 Nasdaq crash). BUT the honest empirical record on top-CALLING is weak: a divergence is a condition, not a timing signal - it can persist for weeks, months, or over a year, produces frequent false positives during ordinary corrections, and tops are inherently hard to time. Practitioner consensus is to treat divergence as a yellow flag and wait for a PRICE trigger (a 50-DMA or trendline break) before acting. The important asymmetry: bullish breadth THRUSTS off washout lows (Zweig-type surge from <40% to >61.5% of stocks advancing within ~10 days) are far more reliable than bearish divergences - they are rare (~18 since 1945) but historically preceded ~23% average 12-month S&P gains with a near-perfect record, because bottoms follow repeatable patterns and the market drifts up over time (fewer false positives than tops). On the level side, the share of stocks above the 200-DMA is the regime gauge: >70% = broad heal
key_points: Breadth measures participation the index level hides; narrowing participation (A-D lower high vs index new high, falling % above 200-DMA) is the top-warning pattern but historically an unreliable TIMING tool

A breadth divergence is a CONDITION, not a timing signal - it can persist for months and gives many false positives; use it to lower aggression, never as a standalone short or stand-down. Wait for a price trigger (50-DMA break) to act

Asymmetry: bullish breadth THRUSTS off lows are far more reliable than bearish divergences at tops - bottoms follow repeatable patterns, tops do not; the thrust is the higher-confidence, press-harder signal
% of stocks above 200-DMA is the regime gauge: >70% broad uptrend, 30-70% neutral, <30% broken; >85-90% is stretched (pullback risk, not a sell)

pct_beating_spy_1m < ~40% means the index is carried by a minority however healthy the level looks - the sharpest single fragility read (2023-24: % above 50-DMA fell ~80%->40% under narrow mega-cap leadership)
Empirical caveat is genuine: divergences 'called' 1987/2000/2007/2021 but also fired falsely often; only combine with price confirmation
entries.how_to_apply: In the regime step (step #1, the aggression dial), read market_breadth.universe FIRST for participation, starting with pct_beating_spy_1m: under ~40% treat the tape as neutral-to-fragile even when benchmark_trend reads supportive, and shift toward smaller size and a different KIND of setup (catalyst, value, diversifier) rather than more of the leadership - exactly the 'act cautious' response CLAUDE.md and momentum_health 'softening' already prescribe. Treat a breadth divergence (index near highs while pct_above_200dma is falling / advance_decline_ratio deteriorating) as a yellow flag that lowers aggression, NEVER as a reason to reject an otherwise-clean fat pitch and never as a stand-down - it is a condition not a timing signal and the only hard regime block is the SPY-below-200-DMA regime gate (this mirrors KB-4213529672: a standing condition must not become an unwritten veto). Conversely, weight bullish breadth EXPANSION as the higher-confidence asymmetric signal: when pct_above_200dma crosses back above 50% and pct_beating_spy_1m rises through 40-50% (a broadening/thrust regime), that is when to press hardest and take full-size fat pitches.
